ULS should remain in the node universe as a pure testing/certification plus supply-chain transparency software candidate; later layers must verify software materiality and policy-linked revenue sensitivity.
TRI is a reference leader, not the alpha lane; ONESOURCE Global Trade is directly relevant but likely diluted inside a much larger information-services business.

NOTE is a speculative shadow candidate only: business-line relevance to policy/tariff intelligence is real, but OTC status, micro-cap size, and financing risk require strict gating before any later-layer survival.
Key node-pure companies appear private or no longer standard listed: Exiger, Interos, Altana, Assent, TrusTrace, and Dun & Bradstreet. Public substitutes may be less pure than private leaders.
DSGX is the cleanest public-market mapping found for trade-compliance and denied-party-screening exposure inside the supply-chain visibility/compliance node.

DNB is a plausible underfollowed supplier-risk data candidate, but the key verification is whether supplier-risk and compliance products are material enough to move consolidated results.
NOTE is a speculative shadow candidate due to micro-cap risk and uncertain monetization, despite thematic overlap with regulatory and supply-chain risk intelligence.

Policy complexity appears to create demand for software and data layers that prove who suppliers are, where goods originate, whether counterparties are restricted, and whether products meet required standards.

Private companies such as Exiger, Altana, Assent, Everstream, and specialized forced-labor or supply-chain-illumination vendors may be closer to the pure chokepoint than many public companies; use them as competitive benchmarks in later layers.
DSGX should remain on the public-candidate watchlist as the cleanest US-listed trade-compliance and customs-software proxy for tariff/sanctions/customs-complexity demand.
ULS and ITRKY belong in the testing/inspection/certification gate lane; later layers should test whether supply-chain transparency and compliance tools are material enough versus broad TIC revenue.

NOTE is a speculative micro-cap policy/regulatory data proxy and should not survive Layer 2 unless evidence shows direct trade, procurement, sanctions, tariff, or supply-chain regulatory monitoring use cases.

Many pure-play supply-chain illumination companies appear private, including Altana, Exiger, Interos, and Z2Data; public-market mapping may require second-order proxies such as trade-compliance software, TIC firms, data providers, and government IT contractors.

The key falsification test for this node is whether policy/regulatory complexity converts into measurable revenue growth for compliance modules, supplier-risk products, certification databases, or inspection/audit volumes rather than remaining a narrative tailwind.
DSGX is the cleanest public mid-cap candidate found for the trade-compliance and tariff/sanctions/data portion of the supply-chain visibility node.
ULS is a large-cap reference name for TIC/certification exposure; keep as context anchor, but later layers should test whether policy-linked compliance is material versus generic testing demand.
ICFI is an underfollowed small-cap government-services candidate with evidence of forced-labor supply-chain tracing and policy implementation exposure, but not a pure software/data play.

NOTE is a speculative micro-cap exception for policy/regulatory intelligence exposure; must be heavily filtered for liquidity, listing status, balance-sheet risk, and real supply-chain-compliance use cases.

Several highly relevant pure-play supply-chain illumination vendors appear private rather than public, including Interos, Exiger, Everstream Analytics, and Altana; public-market mapping may therefore require second-order proxies.
Dun & Bradstreet would have been a strong supplier-risk/data candidate, but it is no longer US-listed after the completed Clearlake acquisition and NYSE delisting in August 2025.

node: Supply-chain visibility, traceability, compliance, and sourcing-resilience tools
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expanded the direct public-company universe for supply-chain visibility and compliance tools. The strongest public-market fit is not defense primes or tariff beneficiaries directly, but software/data/testing firms that help companies and agencies prove origin, supplier risk, customs compliance, certification, and regulatory readiness. Reference lane: Thomson Reuters as a large-cap global trade compliance software anchor. Underfollowed lane: Descartes Systems, UL Solutions, and a speculative OTC micro-cap FiscalNote. Important private-company coverage gaps remain: Exiger, Interos, Altana, Assent, TrusTrace, and Dun & Bradstreet are highly relevant but not currently standard U.S.-listed equities. Layer 1B expansion for the underfollowed lane finds that the investable universe is not dominated by obvious defense primes or mega-cap software platforms. The more relevant chokepoint candidates are trade-compliance software, denied-party screening, supplier-risk data, product certification, and regulatory-intelligence providers. Core demand driver is policy complexity: tariffs, sanctions, forced-labor restrictions, defense sourcing rules, and board-level supply-chain visibility requirements. Evidence is strongest for Descartes, Dun & Bradstreet, UL Solutions, and FiscalNote as public-market mappings, but later layers must verify how much revenue is directly tied to policy-linked supply-chain compliance rather than generic logistics, credit data, TIC, or SaaS demand.
